title: Do Hangover Patches Work? An Honest Look at Bytox and Vitamin Patches
excerpt: Do hangover patches like Bytox actually work? An ingredient-by-ingredient look at B-vitamin patches, why skin blocks most vitamins, what users report, and better options.
metaDescription: Do hangover patches like Bytox work? What the evidence says about B-vitamin patches, skin absorption, each ingredient, and better options to try instead.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** there is no good evidence that hangover patches work. Not one published clinical trial has tested a B-vitamin hangover patch (Bytox or any other brand) against a placebo patch. On top of that, the basic science works against them: your skin is built to keep water-soluble molecules like B vitamins out, and the one study that compared vitamin patches with ordinary pills found the patch users ended up with more deficiencies, not fewer. If you want B vitamins, a cheap tablet does the job better. If you want something aimed at a hangover, your money is better spent on water, food, pacing, and an oral supplement that actually has some human data behind it.

**The quick verdict:** hangover patches are mostly harmless, but they're a weak and expensive way to deliver vitamins, and there's no good evidence the vitamins themselves prevent hangovers anyway. If one has seemed to help you, it's worth asking whether the real difference was the glass of water you drank, the dinner you ate, or simply believing it would work.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. Talk to a doctor if you drink heavily on a regular basis, you have liver or kidney disease, you are pregnant, or you take prescription medicine. Seek urgent care for signs of alcohol poisoning: confusion, vomiting while drowsy, slow or irregular breathing, seizures, or someone you can't wake up. In an emergency, call 911.

## What Is a Hangover Patch?

A hangover patch is a small adhesive sticker, usually about the size of a large bandage, that you put on clean, hair-free skin before or while you drink. The idea is that vitamins and plant extracts soaked into the adhesive seep through your skin into your bloodstream over the next several hours, topping up nutrients that alcohol depletes and leaving you feeling better the next morning.

**Bytox** is the best-known brand in the US, but there are plenty of others sold on Amazon, at gas stations, at festivals, and through social media ads, often marketed as "party patches" or "recovery patches." The formulas vary, but most are built around the same core:

- **A B-vitamin complex:** thiamine (B1), riboflavin (B2), niacin (B3), pantothenic acid (B5), pyridoxine (B6), biotin (B7), folate (B9), and cobalamin (B12)
- **Sometimes extra ingredients** such as vitamin C, plant extracts (milk thistle and others), antioxidants, or, in a few newer products, a small amount of DHM

Labels change often, so check the current one before you buy. But whatever the exact list, every patch rests on two separate claims, and both need to be true for the product to work:

1. **The ingredients actually get through your skin** in useful amounts.
2. **Those ingredients actually reduce hangovers** once they're in your body.

Let's take them one at a time.

## The Core Problem: Can Vitamins Get Through Your Skin?

This is the part the marketing skips. Your skin is not a sponge. Its outer layer, called the **stratum corneum**, is a thin wall of flattened dead cells glued together with fats. Its whole job is to stop water, chemicals, and germs from getting in, and to stop your body's water from getting out. It's very good at that job.

### Which molecules can get through skin?

Real, FDA-approved drug patches do exist, and they work well. Nicotine patches, fentanyl patches for severe pain, scopolamine patches for motion sickness, and estrogen and testosterone patches are all common. But these drugs share a specific set of traits that make them suited to the skin:

- **They're small.** Dermatology researchers often cite a rough guideline called the "500 Dalton rule" (proposed by Bos and Meinardi in *Experimental Dermatology* in 2000): molecules much heavier than about 500 daltons, a unit of molecular weight, struggle to pass through healthy skin.
- **They dissolve in fat.** Because the skin barrier is made largely of fats, molecules that are fat-soluble (lipophilic) slip through far more easily than water-soluble ones.
- **They work at tiny doses.** Even a good patch only delivers a small amount of drug per day. That's fine for fentanyl or nicotine, which act at microgram-to-low-milligram doses, but it's a real limit for anything you need in larger amounts.
- **The patch is engineered for it.** Approved patches use carefully designed reservoirs, chemical penetration enhancers, and drug concentrations that are tested to prove a specific amount reaches the blood.

### How B vitamins measure up

B vitamins fail most of these tests:

- **They're water-soluble.** Every B vitamin dissolves in water, not fat. That's the opposite of what the skin barrier lets through.
- **Some are big.** Vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin) weighs about 1,355 daltons, nearly three times the rough cut-off. It's one of the least likely molecules in the patch to cross intact skin.
- **Several carry an electric charge.** Thiamine, for example, is a charged molecule, and charged molecules have an especially hard time crossing the fatty layer of the skin.

Smaller B vitamins like niacin and B6 are under the size cut-off, so it's not impossible for small amounts to get in. But "a small amount might get through" is a long way from "this delivers a meaningful dose." And critically, hangover patch makers generally don't publish blood-level data showing how much of each vitamin reaches your bloodstream. Approved drug patches have to prove that. Vitamin patches don't.

### What the one real comparison found

The most useful study on vitamin patches didn't involve hangovers at all. A 2019 study published in *Obesity Surgery* followed people after weight-loss surgery, a group that needs lifelong vitamin supplements because their gut absorbs nutrients poorly. Doctors compared people using a multivitamin patch with people taking oral multivitamins. After a year, the patch group was **more likely to be deficient** in several nutrients, including vitamin D, than the people taking pills.

That's a striking result, because these patients had every reason to benefit from a non-oral route. If patches couldn't keep their vitamin levels up over twelve months, it's hard to see how a single patch worn for one night would produce a noticeable effect.

### "But I felt the difference"

Some patch makers point out that vitamins are absorbed through the gut poorly when you drink, so skin is a "better" route. There's a grain of truth in the first part: heavy, long-term drinking does interfere with how the gut absorbs thiamine and folate. But a patch doesn't fix that, because the skin barrier is a much bigger obstacle than a few drinks are to your gut. For a healthy person on a single night out, an oral B-complex taken with food is absorbed reasonably well, and you know roughly what dose you're getting.

## Ingredient by Ingredient: What Each One Could (and Couldn't) Do

Let's assume, generously, that a patch did deliver its ingredients. Would they help a hangover? Here's what's known about each common ingredient.

### Thiamine (vitamin B1)

**Why it's included:** alcohol interferes with thiamine absorption and use, and chronic heavy drinkers are at real risk of serious thiamine deficiency. In its severe form this causes Wernicke's encephalopathy, a medical emergency.

**The reality:** that risk is about long-term heavy drinking and poor diet, not a single night out. There's no good evidence that extra thiamine prevents or eases a hangover in people who aren't deficient. If you drink heavily most days, thiamine matters, but the answer is a conversation with your doctor and a reliable oral or injected supplement, not a sticker.

### Riboflavin (vitamin B2)

**Why it's included:** it helps your cells turn food into energy.

**The reality:** riboflavin deficiency is uncommon in people who eat a normal diet, and there's no research linking riboflavin to hangover relief. Large oral doses mostly turn your urine bright yellow.

### Niacin (vitamin B3)

**Why it's included:** niacin is used to build NAD+, a molecule your liver needs to break down alcohol.

**The reality:** this is one of the more interesting ingredients on paper. In a 2019 study in the *Journal of Clinical Medicine*, researchers in the Netherlands who study hangovers (Verster and colleagues) asked drinkers about their usual diet and found that people with higher dietary intake of niacin and zinc reported somewhat less severe hangovers. That's a survey finding. It shows an association, not proof that taking niacin prevents a hangover, and it was about food intake, not a patch. Your body also makes NAD+ from other sources, so there's no clear reason to think extra niacin on a single night speeds alcohol breakdown in a well-fed person.

### Pantothenic acid (vitamin B5)

**Why it's included:** it's part of coenzyme A, which takes part in many metabolic steps, including some involved in processing alcohol's by-products.

**The reality:** deficiency is extremely rare, and there's no human hangover research on it.

### Pyridoxine (vitamin B6)

**Why it's included:** this is the B vitamin with the best-known hangover link.

**The reality:** the link comes from a small 1970s study of **pyritinol**, a synthetic relative of B6, which found less severe hangover symptoms in the group taking large oral doses. Pyritinol isn't the same thing as the pyridoxine in a patch, the study was small and old, and it used doses taken by mouth. Systematic reviews of hangover remedies have generally treated this as weak, unconfirmed evidence. B6 is also one of the few B vitamins you can take too much of: high oral doses over long periods can cause nerve damage, which is a good reason not to stack multiple B6-heavy products.

### Biotin (vitamin B7)

**Why it's included:** mostly, it seems, because it rounds out the "full B-complex" label.

**The reality:** there's no plausible hangover role for biotin. One practical note: high-dose biotin can interfere with some lab blood tests, including certain thyroid and heart tests. If you're having blood work done, mention any biotin supplement to your doctor.

### Folate (vitamin B9)

**Why it's included:** heavy drinkers often have low folate.

**The reality:** like thiamine, low folate is a long-term heavy-drinking problem, not a one-night problem. It's important for anyone who could become pregnant, but that's an everyday diet-and-supplement issue, best handled with an oral supplement your doctor recommends.

### Cobalamin (vitamin B12)

**Why it's included:** it's associated with energy in popular marketing, and B12 shots are a fixture of IV and "wellness" clinics.

**The reality:** B12 is the least likely ingredient in the patch to get through your skin because of its size. And unless you're deficient, more B12 doesn't give you more energy. Your body stores B12 for years, which is why a one-night dose wouldn't change much even if it were absorbed.

### Vitamin C and antioxidants

**Why they're included:** alcohol metabolism creates oxidative stress, so antioxidants sound like a natural fit.

**The reality:** vitamin C is water-soluble, which again makes skin delivery unlikely. There's no good human evidence that antioxidant patches reduce hangovers.

### Milk thistle and other plant extracts

**Why they're included:** milk thistle has a long history as a liver herb.

**The reality:** milk thistle's active compounds are poorly absorbed even when taken by mouth, and the human evidence for liver benefits is mixed. There's no good reason to expect a meaningful amount to reach your liver from a patch. If you're interested in liver herbs, our [best liver supplements guide](/never-hungover/best-liver-supplements) looks at the oral evidence.

### DHM in a patch

A few newer patches list dihydromyricetin (DHM). DHM is the ingredient this site focuses on, so it's worth being clear: **we're not aware of any published evidence that DHM gets through skin in useful amounts.** DHM is fairly water-loving and is known to be poorly absorbed even when swallowed, which is why oral products use doses of several hundred milligrams to 1,000 mg or more. A patch can't hold anywhere near that much. If you want to try DHM, take it by mouth.

## Even If Patches Worked, Would B Vitamins Fix a Hangover?

This is the second problem, and it gets less attention than it deserves. A hangover isn't primarily a vitamin deficiency. Researchers think it comes from several things happening at once:

- **Your immune system reacting to alcohol**, producing inflammation that makes you feel sick and achy
- **Acetaldehyde**, a toxic by-product made when your liver breaks down alcohol
- **Disrupted sleep**, because alcohol knocks out deep and REM sleep in the second half of the night
- **Dehydration and stomach irritation**
- **Congeners**, extra compounds found in darker drinks such as bourbon and red wine
- **Low blood sugar** in some people

B vitamins don't directly address any of these. That's why large reviews of hangover remedies have come up empty-handed for vitamins. A 2005 systematic review in the *BMJ* concluded there was no compelling evidence that any conventional or complementary remedy prevented or treated hangovers. A more recent systematic review published in *Addiction* in 2022 by researchers at the University of Bristol looked at a wide range of remedies and judged the overall evidence to be of very low quality, with no remedy proven to work well. Vitamins didn't stand out in either review.

So the honest picture is: weak evidence that B vitamins help hangovers when swallowed, and weak evidence that patches deliver B vitamins at all. Multiply two weak links together and you get a very weak chain.

## Why Do So Many People Swear by Them?

If you read Amazon reviews or Reddit threads about Bytox and similar patches, you'll find a real split. A fair summary of what users say:

**The positive side:**

- Some people report waking up noticeably better, and a few say they now won't go out without one.
- People like the convenience. There's no pill to remember the next morning, and a patch is easy to put on before going out.
- Fans often describe it as part of a routine that also includes water and food.

**The negative side:**

- Many people report no difference at all, especially after heavier nights.
- Patches peeling off, especially when sweating, dancing, or showering, is a common complaint.
- Some people get skin redness or itching from the adhesive.
- The price per night is high compared with a bottle of oral B-complex tablets, which can cost just a few cents a day.
- A lot of skeptics point out that the people who are careful enough to wear a patch are often the same people who drink water and eat before bed.

That last point is the key to understanding the glowing reviews. There are several reasons someone could genuinely feel better while wearing a patch that does nothing:

1. **The placebo effect.** Expecting to feel better really does change how symptoms feel, especially for subjective things like headache, fatigue, and mood.
2. **The routine effect.** Putting on a "hangover patch" is a reminder that you're trying to avoid a hangover. People who do that often drink a bit less or more slowly, and drink more water.
3. **Night-to-night variation.** Hangovers vary a lot even with similar drinking, depending on food, sleep, what you drank, and how fast. A good morning after wearing a patch feels like proof, but it could easily have been a good morning anyway.
4. **Nobody tests it fairly at home.** To know if a patch works, you'd need to compare identical nights with and without it, without knowing which was which. That's what clinical trials do, and none has been done for these products.

None of this means the people who like their patches are foolish. It means personal experience can't separate the patch from everything else that happened that night.

## Are Hangover Patches Regulated?

Not in the way most people assume. Under US law, a dietary supplement is defined as something taken by mouth, so a vitamin patch doesn't fit neatly into the supplement category. Real drug patches, like nicotine or scopolamine patches, are regulated as drugs and must prove to the FDA that they deliver their medicine in the claimed amount. Vitamin patches sold for hangovers generally haven't gone through any approval process, and no agency checks that they deliver what the label says.

In practice, that means:

- There's no requirement to show the vitamins reach your blood.
- Label amounts tell you what's in the adhesive, not what gets into you.
- Quality can vary between brands and even between batches.

## Are Hangover Patches Safe?

For most healthy adults, they're unlikely to cause harm, mostly because so little probably gets absorbed. The realistic risks are:

- **Skin irritation or an allergic reaction** to the adhesive or plant extracts. Remove the patch if your skin gets red, itchy, or blistered.
- **False confidence.** The bigger risk is behavioral. A patch can make people feel protected and drink more than they otherwise would. No patch, pill, or drink lowers your blood alcohol level or makes you safer to drive.
- **Stacking.** If you also take an oral multivitamin, a B-complex, and an energy drink loaded with B vitamins, it's worth adding up your B6 intake over time.
- **Biotin and lab tests.** As mentioned above, tell your doctor if you use biotin before blood work.

If you're pregnant, have a skin condition, or take prescription medicine, check with your doctor or pharmacist before using any supplement product, including a patch.

## Hangover Patch vs Pills: How They Compare

Here's a straightforward side-by-side of a typical B-vitamin hangover patch and an ordinary oral B-complex tablet:

| | Hangover patch | Oral B-complex |
|---|---|---|
| Proven to deliver vitamins to the blood | No published data for hangover patches | Yes, well established |
| Clinical trials for hangovers | None | Very limited, mostly weak |
| Typical cost | Usually around $1 to $3 per patch | Often a few cents per tablet |
| Dose you actually get | Unknown | Close to the label amount |
| Main downsides | Peeling, skin irritation, unknown absorption | Can upset an empty stomach, bright yellow urine |

If B vitamins appeal to you, the pill wins on every measurable point. And if you're a regular heavy drinker who is genuinely worried about thiamine or folate, a pill (or treatment from a doctor) is the only route with evidence behind it.

## What About the "Best Hangover Patch"?

People often search for the best hangover patch, Bytox reviews, or the best hangover patch on Amazon. The honest answer is that there's no reliable way to rank them, because none of them has published evidence that it works. Ranking patches by star rating mostly ranks them by marketing and placebo. Since the active ingredients are so similar from brand to brand, the main real differences are price, how well the adhesive sticks, and whether your skin tolerates it.

If you've decided to try one anyway, here's how to be a smarter buyer:

- **Ignore "absorbs 10 times better" claims** unless the company shows published blood-level data. We're not aware of any brand that does.
- **Check the full ingredient list** for anything you're allergic to.
- **Compare cost per night** with an oral B-complex. If the patch costs 20 to 50 times more, that's what you're paying for convenience and packaging.
- **Treat it as optional.** Don't change how much you drink because you're wearing one.

## What Actually Helps a Hangover (With Better Evidence)

No remedy is a cure, and the only guaranteed way to avoid a hangover is to drink less. But some steps have more support than a patch:

- **Drink less, and more slowly.** Hangover severity tracks closely with how much you drink and how fast your blood alcohol rises. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits that matter most.
- **Eat a real meal first.** Food slows how fast alcohol is absorbed.
- **Alternate with water** and have a glass or two before bed. It won't cure a hangover, but dehydration makes headaches and fatigue worse.
- **Choose clearer drinks.** Lighter drinks like vodka and gin tend to have fewer congeners than whiskey, brandy, or red wine. Interestingly, the order you drink in doesn't seem to matter much: a 2019 crossover trial from Witten/Herdecke University, published in the *American Journal of Clinical Nutrition*, found that "beer before wine" or "wine before beer" made no real difference to next-day hangover. Total intake did.
- **Protect your sleep.** Skip the last drink if it's getting late, since alcohol fragments the second half of the night.
- **Consider oral supplements with at least some human data.** The evidence here is still limited, but it's better than for patches. For example, a small randomized trial published in *Alcohol and Alcoholism* in 2020 found that oral L-cysteine reduced some hangover symptoms compared with placebo. Our [hangover supplements guide](/never-hungover/hangover-supplements-complete-guide-what-actually-works-2025) walks through each popular option and how strong (or weak) its evidence really is.

## Where DHM Fits In

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree, *Hovenia dulcis*. It drew attention after a 2012 study in the *Journal of Neuroscience* found it reduced signs of alcohol intoxication and withdrawal in rats. Later lab and animal research has looked at how it may affect alcohol metabolism and the liver.

To be straightforward about it: the human evidence for DHM is still limited, and it isn't a proven hangover cure either. We think it's a more reasonable thing to try than a vitamin patch, for two reasons. It's taken by mouth, which avoids the skin-absorption problem entirely, and it's aimed at how the body handles alcohol rather than at replacing vitamins most people aren't short of.

If you want to try it, timing and dose matter more than brand. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take, and our [DHM timing guide](/never-hungover/when-to-take-dhm-timing-guide-2025) explains when to take it relative to drinking. Popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which combines DHM with L-cysteine, and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20).

As with any supplement, check with your doctor first if you take prescription medicine or have liver disease, and don't use DHM (or anything else) as a reason to drink more.

## The Bottom Line

- **No clinical trial has shown that a hangover patch works.** That includes Bytox and every other brand we're aware of.
- **Skin is a strong barrier against water-soluble vitamins.** B12 in particular is too large to pass through easily, and patch makers don't publish data showing how much reaches the blood.
- **The one real comparison went against patches.** In the 2019 *Obesity Surgery* study, people using vitamin patches were more likely to become deficient than people taking pills.
- **B vitamins aren't a proven hangover fix even when swallowed.** Hangovers are mostly about inflammation, acetaldehyde, poor sleep, and dehydration.
- **Patches are probably harmless but poor value.** The main risks are skin irritation and the false confidence to drink more.
- **Better bets:** drink less and slower, eat, hydrate, and if you want a supplement, choose an oral one with at least some human evidence.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Do hangover patches actually work?**

There's no good evidence that they do. No published clinical trial has tested a B-vitamin hangover patch against a placebo, and the skin is a strong barrier against water-soluble vitamins. A 2019 study in people after weight-loss surgery found that those using vitamin patches were more likely to become deficient than those taking pills. Any benefit people notice is more likely due to placebo, drinking water, eating, or a lighter night.

**Does Bytox work?**

Bytox hasn't published clinical trial results showing it reduces hangovers or that its vitamins reach the bloodstream in meaningful amounts. User reviews are mixed: some people say they feel better, while many notice no difference or complain about patches peeling off. Based on the available evidence, we can't recommend it as an effective hangover remedy.

**Can vitamins be absorbed through the skin?**

Only to a very limited degree, and it depends on the molecule. Skin lets through small, fat-soluble molecules best, which is why nicotine and some hormones work as patches. B vitamins and vitamin C are water-soluble, and B12 is about three times larger than the rough size limit for passing through skin. Small amounts of some vitamins may get in, but there's no evidence a hangover patch delivers a useful dose.

**Are vitamin patches better than pills?**

No. Oral B vitamins are absorbed reliably, are cheap, and you know roughly what dose you're getting. Patches cost far more per dose and have no published proof of how much reaches your blood. The one head-to-head study we know of (published in Obesity Surgery in 2019) found patch users were more likely to end up deficient than pill users.

**What is the best hangover patch?**

There isn't a meaningful "best" one, because none has evidence that it works. Most contain a similar B-vitamin mix, so the real differences are price, how well the adhesive sticks, and whether it irritates your skin. If you want to try B vitamins, an oral B-complex is cheaper and more reliable. For hangover-specific options, see our hangover supplements guide.

**Are hangover patches safe?**

For most healthy adults they're unlikely to cause harm, mainly because so little is probably absorbed. Possible problems include skin irritation from the adhesive and, more importantly, feeling protected enough to drink more. No patch lowers your blood alcohol level or makes it safe to drive. If you're pregnant, have a skin condition, or take prescription medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist first.

**Do B vitamins help with hangovers?**

The evidence is weak. A 2019 survey-based study linked higher dietary niacin and zinc intake with somewhat milder hangovers, and a small 1970s study found benefits from pyritinol, a synthetic relative of vitamin B6. Neither proves that taking B vitamins prevents hangovers. Thiamine and folate matter for people who drink heavily on a regular basis, but that's a long-term health issue to discuss with a doctor, not a one-night fix.

**Is a hangover patch better than DHM?**

They work in completely different ways, and neither is a proven cure. DHM is taken by mouth and targets how the body handles alcohol, with promising animal research and limited human data. Vitamin patches face the extra problem that their ingredients may not get through the skin at all. If you want to try something, an oral supplement like DHM, taken at the right time and dose, is the more reasonable choice.
